artifacts.title: Agency Policy: Confidentiality in Communicable Disease Case Management
artifacts.author: Douglas County Health Department
artifacts.body: Per state communicable disease reporting statute and department policy, personal health information collected during TB case management and contact investigation is confidential and used solely for disease control purposes. Information is not shared with employers, landlords, schools, or immigration enforcement agencies absent a court order. Interpreter services are available at no cost and declining them does not affect care or confidentiality protections.

objectives.text: Elicit true medication adherence using nonjudgmental, trust-building questioning rather than accepting an initial 'I take it every day' statement at face value, then cross-check against the pharmacy fill record.

Elicit medication side effects (orange urine, nausea) through sensitive follow-up questioning as the probable driver of self-discontinuation, and distinguish benign expected effects from signs requiring escalation to the prescribing clinician.
Correct a key misunderstanding about latent versus active TB infection and the rationale for completing treatment despite feeling well.
Address confidentiality concerns regarding employer and immigration status using accurate agency policy information, within the scope of public health nursing practice.

Screen for alcohol use given its relevance to hepatotoxicity risk with rifampin, and refer to the prescribing clinician/TB program for further clinical evaluation (e.g., repeat liver function tests) before any restart, recognizing that determining restart readiness is outside PHN scope.
Continue contact investigation follow-up by identifying untested household contacts and planning outreach, consistent with the public health nursing scope for communicable disease case management.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient states he is taking the rifampin every day as prescribed.
mismatches.recordEvidence: Pharmacy fill history shows only one 30-day supply (30 capsules) filled five weeks ago, which if taken daily would have run out by about week 4; a 4-month course would require roughly 3 more 30-day fills, and the record shows 3 refills still remaining unused with no subsequent fills logged.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Self-reported adherence often overstates actual medication-taking; pharmacy refill history is an objective cross-check (a 30-day supply with no refills since week 1 cannot cover 5 weeks of daily dosing), and discrepancies should be explored supportively rather than confrontationally.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient believes a couple of his housemates have not yet been tested.
mismatches.recordEvidence: Contact investigation log shows one contact (Contact 4) has a pending test and two contacts (5 and 6) have not been tested, with documented outreach attempts, confirming the gap but with more detail/nuance than the patient's general impression.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Patient awareness of contact testing status may be incomplete; the nurse should verify current outreach status directly from the case log rather than relying solely on the index patient's secondhand information.

scenario.studentBrief: You are a public health nursing student making a scheduled video follow-up visit for Pedro Alvarado, 36, who was identified as a contact of a person with infectious pulmonary TB. He tested positive on an interferon-gamma release assay with a clear chest X-ray (latent TB infection) and started daily rifampin five weeks ago. Your visit is to check on his treatment progress, screen for side effects or active disease symptoms, address any concerns, and continue contact investigation follow-up for his household.
scenario.chiefComplaint: Scheduled follow-up visit for latent TB infection treatment adherence, 5 weeks after starting rifampin.
scenario.openingLine: Hi, yeah, I know you're calling about the TB pills they put me on.
tasks: Take a focused history of adherence and any symptoms since starting treatment
Review the medication regimen with the patient
Explore any questions or concerns the patient has about his treatment or the contact investigation
Screen for factors relevant to treatment safety and completion
Agree a plan for next steps and follow-up

answerKey.primaryProblem: Nonadherence to latent TB infection (LTBI) treatment (rifampin) due to self-discontinuation after transient side effects, compounded by misunderstanding of latent vs. active disease and confidentiality/immigration concerns; ongoing contact investigation gaps.
differential: Latent TB infection with early treatment discontinuation (consistent with pharmacy fill history showing no refills since the initial 30-day supply)
Mild self-limited rifampin side effects (orange urine discoloration, nausea) now resolved, versus early drug-induced hepatotoxicity requiring clinical evaluation before restart
Progression to active pulmonary TB disease (ruled out today by absence of cough, hemoptysis, fever, night sweats, or weight loss; prior chest X-ray clear)
Alcohol use as a contributing risk factor for hepatotoxicity if rifampin is restarted
keyFindings: Patient reports taking rifampin daily, but pharmacy fill history shows only one 30-day supply filled 5 weeks ago with no subsequent fills, inconsistent with 5 weeks of continuous daily use
On direct, supportive questioning, patient discloses he discontinued rifampin after approximately 2 weeks due to orange urine and nausea, both now resolved, and because he felt well
Denies current symptoms of active TB disease (no cough, hemoptysis, fever, night sweats, weight loss)
On sensitive questioning, reports regular alcohol use (4-5 beers most evenings), a relevant risk factor for hepatotoxicity
With trust established, voices concern that health department information could be shared with employer or immigration authorities
Two household contacts remain untested per the case log, with documented outreach attempts
plan: Provide health education correcting the misunderstanding that absence of symptoms means treatment is unnecessary; explain latent vs. active TB infection in simple terms
Reassure patient using documented agency confidentiality policy that case information is not shared with employers or immigration enforcement, and offer interpreter services again without pressure

Refer back to prescribing clinician/TB program provider for clinical evaluation (including repeat liver function tests given alcohol use and prior side effects) before restarting rifampin; medication restart, dosing, and determination of clinical readiness are outside public health nursing scope and belong to the prescribing clinician
Document adherence gap and side-effect history clearly in the public health case record for the care team
Continue contact investigation: coordinate outreach and testing scheduling for the two untested household contacts, document attempts and barriers

Discuss practical barriers (work schedule, hourly pay with no sick leave) and connect patient with any applicable local resources (e.g., directly observed therapy options, flexible appointment times) to support adherence if treatment resumes
Schedule follow-up contact to confirm whether treatment is resumed and continue monitoring
redFlags: New cough, hemoptysis, fever, night sweats, or weight loss would suggest progression to active TB disease and require urgent escalation

Jaundice, dark urine persisting beyond initial days, severe abdominal pain, or significantly elevated liver enzymes would suggest hepatotoxicity requiring urgent medical evaluation before any restart of rifampin
Continued nonadherence with ongoing close-contact exposure risk to housemates warrants escalation to TB program clinician for consideration of alternative strategies (e.g., directly observed therapy)
educationPoints: Latent TB infection means the bacteria are inactive and not currently making the person sick or contagious, but completing treatment reduces lifetime risk of the infection becoming active, contagious TB disease

Orange/red discoloration of urine, sweat, and tears is an expected, harmless effect of rifampin and does not by itself mean the medication must be stopped, but new side effects should be reported to the care team rather than silently discontinuing
Public health case information is legally protected and is not routinely shared with employers, landlords, or immigration enforcement
Alcohol use increases the risk of liver side effects from rifampin, so clinicians need accurate information about drinking patterns before restarting treatment
Testing household and workplace contacts promptly helps interrupt transmission and protect other people living with the patient

Pharmacy refill history is a useful objective adherence check: a single 30-day fill with no subsequent refills cannot sustain 5 weeks of daily dosing, pointing to a gap the nurse should explore directly with the patient

profile.title: Non-adherence to latent TB treatment in a 36-year-old roofer with side effects and confidentiality concerns
profile.summary: A 36-year-old Guatemalan-born roofer with latent TB infection self-discontinued daily rifampin after two weeks due to orange urine and nausea, misunderstanding that he needs treatment while feeling healthy. He has confidentiality concerns about employer and immigration authorities, drinks 4-5 beers daily (hepatotoxicity risk), and two housemates remain untested. This case teaches non-judgmental adherence assessment, distinguishing benign from serious medication effects, health literacy about latent TB, addressing confidentiality within public health scope, alcohol screening relevant to rifampin safety, and contact investigation follow-up.
profile.setting: Telehealth video visit; patient's shared rental home (kitchen table)
